chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Sulayman ibn Ja'far al-Ja'fari said:

I was with al-Rida (peace be upon him) attending to a need, and I wanted to return to my house, so he said to me, 'Go with me and spend the night at my place.' So I went with him, and he entered his house at sunset. He looked at his servants who were working with clay making beasts of burden and other things, and with them was a black man who was not one of them. He said, 'What is this man doing with you?' They said, 'He assists us and we give him something.' He said, 'Did you agree with him on his wage?' They said, 'No, he is content with what we give him.' He turned to them, striking them with the whip, and was very angry. I said, 'May I be your ransom, why do you burden yourself?' He said, 'I have commanded them more than once that a worker should not work with them until they agree with him on his wage. And know that there is no one who does something for you without an agreement, and then you add to that thing three times its value on top of his wage, except that he thinks you have shortchanged his wage. So when you agree with him and then give him his wage, he praises you for fidelity. But if you add a single grain, he knows that and perceives that you have added to him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on paying wages to workers and the importance of prior agreement?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (AS) corrects his servants' practice of paying a laborer without a prior wage agreement (*muqatadah*), highlighting that even if the worker is initially content, the lack of formal contract can lead to a psychological sense of being shortchanged. The Imam teaches that clear contractual terms ensure the worker feels satisfied and faithful, whereas arbitrary additions may be perceived as insufficient, thereby underscoring the Shia emphasis on justice (*adl*) and transparency in economic transactions.
